claims.text: asyncio.Queue is a first in, first out queue; if maxsize is less than or equal to zero its size is infinite, and if maxsize is greater than 0, await put() blocks when the queue reaches maxsize until an item is removed by get().

claims.text: In CPython 3.14's queues.py, a put() that finds the queue full appends a new Future to the queue's deque of waiting putters and awaits it; get_nowait() wakes the first waiting putter that is not done, and the woken put() checks for room again before adding its item. put_nowait() wakes waiting getters the same way.

claims.text: join() blocks until all items have been received and processed: the count of unfinished tasks goes up whenever an item is added to the queue and goes down whenever a consumer calls task_done(); when it drops to zero, join() unblocks.

claims.text: Queue.shutdown() puts the queue into shutdown mode: later put() calls raise QueueShutDown and blocked put() callers are woken to raise it; with immediate=False, the default, items already in the queue can still be taken with get(), and once the queue is empty, get() raises QueueShutDown.

claims.text: With immediate=True the queue is drained at once, the unfinished count is reduced by the number of items drained, join() callers are unblocked if that count reaches zero, and blocked get() callers raise QueueShutDown; the docs warn that this unblocks join() even when no work was done on the drained items.

claims.text: Google's SRE book says queued requests consume memory and increase latency, that a queue ten times the size of the thread pool can turn a 100 ms request into a 1.1 s one when full, and that for steady traffic a queue of about 50% of the thread pool size or less is usually better, because it rejects excess load early; for bursty traffic it ties the size to the threads in use, the time per request, and the size and frequency of the bursts.
